name: Arrernte religion (Altyerre)

dating.dating_summary: Central Australian regional occupation (Puritjarra, ~35,000-45,000 BP) is regional evidence, not a date for Arrernte ceremonial content specifically; earliest outsider attestation is Spencer and Gillen's 1896 fieldwork (Engwura ceremony), published 1899 — a source that must be read critically, not as neutral, given its documented ethical problems (see claim_spencer_gillen_durkheim_freud_influence); "geomythology" attempts to date oral tradition against deep-time geological/astronomical events are a distinct, more speculative genre that should not be used to assign a specific age to Altyerre content.

earliest_archaeological_evidence.note: Puritjarra rock shelter and comparable Central Australian sites: continuous occupation from ~35,000-45,000 years ago. Regional occupation evidence only.

earliest_written_attestation.note: Baldwin Spencer and Francis James Gillen, field observation of the Engwura ceremony, 1896, published in The Native Tribes of Central Australia (Macmillan, 1899); expanded in The Arunta: A Study of a Stone Age People (Macmillan, 1927).

surviving_manuscript_date.note: T.G.H. Strehlow, Aranda Traditions (Melbourne UP, 1947) and Songs of Central Australia (Angus & Robertson, 1971) — a controversial custodianship case, see claim_strehlow_scandal.

tradition_internal_claim.note: Altyerre (also Altjira/Alcheringa in older transliterations, described in the sourcing as "possibly the most contested word in modern Australian ethnography") situates ceremonial law, songlines, and totemic geography in an atemporal ancestral-creation framework, not expressed as a calendar date.

estimated_oral_origin.method: No specific dating study located for Arrernte ceremonial content. "Geomythology" literature attempting to correlate deep-time geological/astronomical events with Aboriginal oral tradition generally (e.g. arxiv.org/pdf/1009.4251) is a distinct, more speculative genre and should NOT be used to assign a specific age to Altyerre content — flagged explicitly as a likely error mode.

notes: Kinship: the Arrernte subsection ("skin") system has eight named categories, patrilineally dominant for section/subsection and totemic-estate transmission — see claim_arrernte_kinship_radcliffe_brown_levistrauss. This tradition's documentary record is disproportionately shaped by male ethnographers (Spencer, Gillen, Strehlow) — an observation about the surviving record (P13: not automatically a causal suppression claim) — see claim_arrernte_gender_source_bias for the documented corrective (Turner, Green).
